# Overview

# Meta analysis results

## FSC → WBI

Here we will meta analyse the correlations between future
self-continuity and health behaviours.

```{r}
#| label: data-fsc-wbi
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
```

### Model results

```{r}
#| label: meta-fsc-wbi
#| collapse: true
meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$model_fit
```

The random-effects meta-analysis included 27 effect sizes and indicated a
**positive association between future self-continuity and health behaviours**.
The pooled effect size was
$r = 0.22 \;[0.18, 0.26], \; z = 10.50, p < 0.001$.

The magnitude of the effect size was **small**.

In addition, there was little evidence of between study heterogeneity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fsc-wbi
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated heterogeneity statistics for the relationship between future self continuity and health behaviours"
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$hetero_tbl
```

### Funnel plot

```{r}
#| label: funnel-fsc-wbi
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$model_fit |> meta::funnel()
```

```{r}
#| label: edgar-fsc-wbi
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$model_fit |> regtest()
```

Based off the above funnel plot and the results from Edgars regression, we can
conclude there is no evidence of small sample bias or publication bias.

### Forest plot

```{r}
#| label: forest-fsc-wbi
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$model_fit |> forest()
```

### Moderator & Subgroup analysis

Because there was evidence of between study heterogeneity we will run a set of
subgroup analyses and meta-regressions of the relationship between future
self continuity and health behaviours.

#### Subgroup analyses

::: {.callout-tip}
## Is there a different effect based off sample type?
:::

First let's look at the results we get when we only consider **community**
samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-1a
#| collapse: true

sub_1a <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = sample == "community",
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_1a
```

And then only for **student** samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-1b
#| collapse: true

sub_1b <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = sample == "student",
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_1b
```

Let's compare both sets of results now

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-test-1
#| collapse: true

# Combine both sets of results
sample_results <- tibble(
  sample = c("community", "student"),
  estimate = c(coef(sub_1a), coef(sub_1b)),
  std_error = c(se(sub_1a), se(sub_1b)),
  tau_sq = c(sub_1a$tau2, sub_1b$tau2)
)

# Fit a fixed effects model between the studies
rma(estimate, sei = std_error, mods = ~ sample, method = "FE", data = sample_results)
```

The subgroup analysis based off sample type was non-significant,
$Q(1)   =  0.29, p  = 0.589$. The effects from community samples
$(r_{avg } =  .21 [0.16, 0.26]; k =  21)$ were not significantly different from
those obtained from the student samples
$(r_{avg}  = .23 [0.19, 0.28]; k  =  6$.

---

::: {.callout-note}
## Is there a different effect based off being a lab study or not?
:::

First let's look at the results we get when we only consider **lab**
samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-2a
#| collapse: true

sub_2a <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = lab_study == TRUE,
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_2a
```

And then only for **published** samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-2b
#| collapse: true

sub_2b <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = lab_study == FALSE,
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_2b
```

Let's compare both sets of results now

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-test-2
#| collapse: true

# Combine both sets of results
lab_results <- tibble(
  sample = c("lab", "published"),
  estimate = c(coef(sub_2a), coef(sub_2b)),
  std_error = c(se(sub_2a), se(sub_2b)),
  tau_sq = c(sub_2a$tau2, sub_2b$tau2)
)

# Fit a fixed effects model between the studies
rma(estimate, sei = std_error, mods = ~ sample, method = "FE", data = lab_results)
```

The subgroup analysis based off being a lab or published study was also
non-significant, $Q(1)   =  0.99, p  = 0.319$. The effects from lab samples
$(r_{avg } =  .20 [0.18, 0.23]; k =  21)$ were not significantly different from
those obtained from the published samples
$(r_{avg}  = .29 [0.13, 0.45]; k  = 6$.


---

::: {.callout-note}
## Is there a different effect based off FSC measure?
:::

As there is only one experimental study in the data, we will exclude this from
the analysis and only look at the differences between **single-item** and
**multi-item** samples

First let's look at the results we get when we only consider **single item**
samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-3a
#| collapse: true

sub_3a <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = fsc_measure == "single-item",
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_3a
```

And then only for **multi-item** samples.

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-3b
#| collapse: true

sub_3b <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  subset = fsc_measure == "multi-item",
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

sub_3b
```

Let's compare both sets of results now

```{r}
#| label: subgroup-test-3
#| collapse: true

# Combine both sets of results
measure_results <- tibble(
  sample = c("single-item", "multi-item"),
  estimate = c(coef(sub_3a), coef(sub_3b)),
  std_error = c(se(sub_3a), se(sub_3b)),
  tau_sq = c(sub_3a$tau2, sub_3b$tau2)
)

# Fit a fixed effects model between the studies
rma(
  estimate,
  sei = std_error,
  mods = ~sample,
  method = "FE",
  data = measure_results
)
```

The subgroup analysis based off FSC measure was also
non-significant, $Q(1)  =  0.52, p  = 0.469$. The effects from single-item samples
$(r_{avg } =  .20 [0.17, 0.23]; k =  18)$ were not significantly different from
those obtained from the multi-item samples
$(r_{avg}  = .24 [0.14, 0.35]; k  = 8$.

#### Moderating analysis

::: {.callout-note}
## Is there a moderating effect of gender?
:::

```{r}
#| label: mod-analysis-1a
#| collapse: true

mod_1 <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,
  mods = ~percent_female,
  data = meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean$data
)

mod_1
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## No significant moderating effect of gender
:::

---

::: {.callout-note}

```{r}

mod_2 <- rma(
  yi = z,
  vi = vi,

mod_2
```

:::

## FSC → FSRH

Here we will meta analyse the correlations between future
self-continuity and future self rated health.

```{r}
#| label: data-fsc-fsrh
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$data
```

### Model results

```{r}
#| label: meta-fsc-fsrh
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$model_fit
```

The random-effects meta-analysis included 16 effect sizes and indicated a
**positive association between future self-continuity and future self rated
health**. The pooled effect size was
$r = 0.13 \;[0.10, 0.16], \; z = 7.93, p < 0.001$.

The magnitude of the effect size was **small**.

In addition, there was little evidence of between study heterogeneity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fsc-fsrh
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated heterogeneity statistics for the relationship between future self continuity and poorer future self-rated health"
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$hetero_tbl
```

### Funnel plot

```{r}
#| label: funnel-fsc-fsrh
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$model_fit |> meta::funnel()
```

```{r}
#| label: edgar-fsc-fsrh
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$model_fit |> regtest()
```

Based off the above funnel plot and the results from Edgars regression, we can
conclude there is no evidence of small sample bias or publication bias.

### Forest plot

```{r}
#| label: forest-fsc-fsrh
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_fsrh$model_fit |> forest()
```

## FSRH → WBI

Here we will meta analyse the correlations between poorer future self-rated
health and wellness behaviours

```{r}
#| label: data-fsrh-wbi

```

### Results

```{r}
#| label: meta-fsrh-wbi
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$wbi_mean_fsrh$model_fit
```

The random-effects meta-analysis included 16 effect sizes and indicated a

health**. The pooled effect size was
$r = 0.32 \;[0.28, 0.37], \; z = 15.71, p < 0.001$. The magnitude of the
effect size was **small**.

There was evidence of between study heterogeneity.

Based off the above funnel plot and the results from Edgars regression, we can

## FSC → WBI (Semi partial)

Here we will meta analyse the semi partial correlations between future
self-continuity and well behaviours.

```{r}
#| label: data-fsc-wbi-semi-partial
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean_semi$data
```

### Results

```{r}
#| label: meta-fsc-wbi-semi-partial
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean_semi$model_fit
```

The random-effects meta-analysis included 16 effect sizes and indicated a
**positive association between future self-continuity and wellbeing behaviours**
after accounting for future self-rated health. The pooled semi-partial effect
size was $r = 0.17 \;[0.14, 0.21], \; z = 9.47, p < 0.001$. The magnitude of the
effect size was **small**.

There was little evidence of between study heterogeneity.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-fsc-wbi-semi-partial
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated heterogeneity statistics for the semi partial relationship between future self continuity and wellness behaviours"
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean_semi$hetero_tbl
```

### Funnel plot

```{r}
#| label: funnel-fsc-wbi-semi-partial
#| code-fold: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean_semi$model_fit |> meta::funnel()
```

```{r}
#| label: edgar-fsc-wbi-semi-partial
#| collapse: true

meta_analysis$fsc_wbi_mean_semi$model_fit |> regtest()
```

Based off the above funnel plot and the results from Edgars regression, we can
conclude there is no evidence of small sample bias or publication bias.

### Forest plot

